title: D and f block: configurations, properties and oxidants
subject: Chemistry

chapters.title: Configurations of actual atoms and ions
chapters.formula: Remove outer 4s electrons before 3d for common first-row cations
chapters.script: Welcome to D and F Block Chemistry. This recorded class uses an AI generated Marin voice. Begin with the configuration of the actual species. Neutral chromium is commonly described as an argon core followed by three d five and four s one. Neutral copper has three d ten and four s one beyond that core. These observed configurations are not replaced by an inflexible filling shortcut. For common first row metal cations, remove outer four s electrons before three d electrons. Neutral iron has three d six and four s two. Removing two electrons gives iron two plus with a d six count; removing one more gives iron three plus with d five. Copper two plus has d nine, while zinc two plus has d ten. A transition element has an incomplete d subshell in its atom or an important cation. Zinc's common atom and zinc two plus both have a filled d subshell, so a position in the d block does not automatically make it a typical transition element under that definition.
points: Fe²⁺ · d⁶ · Remove two 4s electrons
Fe³⁺ · d⁵ · Then remove one d electron
Cu²⁺; Zn²⁺ · d⁹; d¹⁰ · Use actual configuration

board.heading: Configurations of actual atoms and ions

chapters.title: Variable oxidation states and environment
chapters.formula: Formal oxidation state is not always a free-ion charge
chapters.script: Outer s and d orbitals in transition elements can have relatively close energies. Different numbers of electrons can therefore participate in bonding, supporting several oxidation states. Their relative stability depends on the element, ligands and medium. Manganese in permanganate has formal oxidation state plus seven, but that does not describe an ordinary free aqueous manganese seven plus ion. The oxygen containing species and its bonding are essential. High oxidation states are often stabilized with oxygen or fluorine, while many later first row compounds favour lower states such as plus two or plus three. Atomic radii also vary less dramatically across much of the transition series than a simple main group comparison might suggest, because increasing nuclear attraction and added d electrons compete. Melting point and ionization trends contain exceptions and should be checked against supplied data. Separate a neutral metal, a dissolved ion and a solid oxide when explaining a property. Sharing the same elemental name does not make those species electronically or structurally identical.
points: Oxidation-state stability · Ligands and medium · Actual compound matters
Mn(VII) in MnO₄⁻ · Oxygen-containing ion · Not free Mn⁷⁺
Across transition row · Nuclear charge and d filling · Trends need data

chapters.title: Unpaired electrons and the spin-only model
chapters.script: In an elementary magnetic model, unpaired electrons give paramagnetism, while an all paired arrangement is diamagnetic. The spin only moment estimate is the square root of the product of n and the quantity n plus two, in Bohr magnetons, where n is the number of unpaired electrons. It is not simply the total d electron count. A specified high spin d five arrangement has five unpaired electrons, so the estimate is the square root of thirty five, about five point nine two Bohr magnetons. Other configurations require the actual orbital arrangement before counting n. Ligand field strength can change the number of unpaired electrons for some d counts, so oxidation state alone is not enough to predict every complex. Orbital contributions and interactions can also make measured moments differ from the spin only estimate. Follow a clear sequence: identify the species, find the oxidation state and d count, use the specified spin environment, then count unpaired electrons. Only after those choices should the numerical formula be applied.
points: High-spin d⁵ · 5 · √35 ≈ 5.92 μB
All paired · 0 · 0 in this model
Different ligand field · Recount n · Do not use d count directly

chapters.title: Colour, charge transfer and catalysis
chapters.formula: d–d absorption is only one source of colour
chapters.script: Many transition compounds absorb visible light through electronic transitions. Splitting of d orbital energies in a ligand environment can allow d to d absorption, but that is not the only mechanism. Charge transfer transitions can give strong colours even when the metal is formally d zero. Permanganate is a familiar coloured example with manganese in oxidation state plus seven and a formal d zero count. A rule that every d zero compound must be colourless therefore fails. Do not infer an exact colour from oxidation state alone: the ligands, structure and allowed transitions matter. Transition metals and their compounds can also act as catalysts through accessible oxidation states, reactive surfaces or intermediate complexes. Small charged metal ions can accept electron pairs from donor ligands and form coordination compounds. These are broad explanations, not guarantees that every metal salt is a useful catalyst. A catalyst changes the reaction pathway and rate under suitable conditions, while the equilibrium constant at fixed temperature remains a thermodynamic property of the reaction.
points: Colour · d–d or charge-transfer absorption · Not d count alone
Permanganate · Charge-transfer contribution · Coloured despite d⁰
Catalysis · Surface or redox pathways · Not every compound works

chapters.title: Alloys, interstitial solids and metallic properties
chapters.formula: Solid-lattice behaviour differs from solution complexes
chapters.script: Many transition metals are dense, strong solids with useful melting points, although the pattern has exceptions. Metallic bonding and the solid structure should be distinguished from the behaviour of a dissolved metal salt. Similar atomic sizes can help different metals occupy a common metallic lattice and form alloys. An alloy need not be a pure molecular compound with one fixed stoichiometric formula. Its properties depend on the elements present, their proportions and the resulting phases. Small atoms such as carbon or nitrogen can occupy spaces in some metal lattices, producing interstitial compounds or related solid phases. These may retain metallic characteristics while becoming harder or showing changed melting behaviour. That does not make an interstitial solid a coordination complex in solution. The same transition element can participate in several kinds of material, with different structures and properties. In a comparison question, identify whether it concerns the elemental metal, an alloy, an interstitial solid or a salt before applying a general statement about transition element chemistry.
points: Alloy · Metallic lattice / phases · Composition affects properties
Interstitial solid · Small atoms in lattice spaces · Hardness may change
Complex ion · Ligands around metal · Different from bulk alloy

chapters.title: Oxidants need a specified medium
chapters.formula: Acidic MnO₄⁻ accepts 5 e⁻; Cr₂O₇²⁻ accepts 6 e⁻
chapters.script: In suitable acidic medium, permanganate is reduced to manganese two plus by accepting five electrons per ion. Dichromate is reduced to two chromium three plus ions by accepting six electrons per dichromate ion. These changes determine redox mole ratios. Permanganate can give other manganese products in other media, so the five electron factor is not universal. Always read the medium and stated reduction product. Preparation of potassium permanganate is conceptually connected with forming manganate and then converting it to permanganate. Potassium dichromate is connected with conversion of chromium ore to chromate followed by the chromate dichromate relationship. Acid base conditions shift that equilibrium: acid favours dichromate relative to chromate under the usual comparison, while alkaline conditions favour chromate. This equilibrium changes the predominant species without itself changing chromium's plus six oxidation state. Distinguish acid base interconversion from reduction to chromium three plus. The two processes use different bookkeeping even though the same element appears in each. Later examples will check both the electron and mole balances explicitly.
points: MnO₄⁻ → Mn²⁺ · 5 per ion · Suitable acidic medium
Cr₂O₇²⁻ → 2 Cr³⁺ · 6 per ion · Reduction, not just pH shift
Chromate ⇌ dichromate · Cr remains +6 · Acid–base interconversion

chapters.title: Lanthanoid contraction and actinoid comparisons
chapters.formula: Growing nuclear charge is incompletely screened by added f electrons
chapters.script: Lanthanoids involve progressive filling of four f orbitals, with plus three a common oxidation state and important exceptions. Across a comparable series of their trivalent ions, size generally decreases because the increasing nuclear charge is not fully screened by added f electrons. This lanthanoid contraction contributes to the chemical similarity of neighbouring members and can make their separation difficult. Similar charge and gradually changing radius support similar behaviour, but do not make every compound identical. Contraction also helps explain the unexpectedly close sizes of some heavier transition pairs, such as zirconium and hafnium. Actinoids involve five f electrons and often show a wider range of accessible oxidation states. Their configurations and bonding require element specific treatment rather than a universal plus three label. When comparing radii, use the same charge and a consistent radius definition; changing both the oxidation state and element at once can obscure the trend. The shielding explanation is a useful cause for a systematic comparison, not permission to ignore the actual species in a table.
points: Lanthanoid(III) series · Imperfect 4f shielding · Gradual contraction
Zr and Hf · Similar sizes · Contraction helps explain
Actinoids · 5f; more varied states · Element-specific chemistry

chapters.title: A method for ion and trend questions
chapters.script: For a metal ion question, begin with the actual species and its oxidation state. Use the neutral configuration as the starting inventory, then remove the appropriate outer electrons to obtain the ion. For common first row cations, removing four s electrons before three d avoids a frequent counting error. Next identify the ligand environment and any specified spin arrangement. The same d count can lead to different magnetic behaviour in different complexes. For redox questions, specify the medium and the final oxidation state before assigning an electron factor. Balance atoms and total charge independently rather than accepting an equation because the coefficients look familiar. For trends, distinguish the first transition series from lanthanoids and actinoids, and identify whether a value belongs to an atom, ion or solid. A tabulated radius or magnetic moment needs its stated definition and conditions. Finally compare the result with basic limits: electron counts must match charge, reaction charge must balance and a spin only unpaired count must fit the available orbitals.
points: Configuration · Actual ion charge · Remove d before outer s
Magnetism · Spin / ligand environment · Use d count as n
Redox · Medium and product · Use one universal factor

chapters.title: Worked magnetic moments for common d counts
chapters.formula: High-spin d⁶: n = 4; high-spin d⁵: n = 5; d⁹: n = 1
chapters.script: Consider iron two plus in a specified high spin d six arrangement. Five d orbitals first receive one electron each, and the sixth makes one pair. Four electrons remain unpaired. The spin only estimate is the square root of four times six, or the square root of twenty four, about four point nine zero Bohr magnetons. High spin iron three plus has d five with five unpaired electrons, giving about five point nine two. In the elementary d nine arrangement for copper two plus, four orbitals are paired and one has an unpaired electron. The estimate is the square root of three, about one point seven three Bohr magnetons. These are model estimates, not exact measured values guaranteed for every solid or complex. If the problem changes ligand field strength, check whether the assumed high spin arrangement remains appropriate before reusing the result. The total d count, the number of unpaired electrons and the numerical moment are three different quantities that should be written separately.
points: Fe²⁺; high-spin d⁶ · 4 · √24 ≈ 4.90 μB
Fe³⁺; high-spin d⁵ · 5 · √35 ≈ 5.92 μB
Cu²⁺; elementary d⁹ · 1 · √3 ≈ 1.73 μB

chapters.title: Worked oxidant amounts and charge balances
chapters.formula: Cr₂O₇²⁻ : Fe²⁺ = 1:6; MnO₄⁻ : Fe²⁺ = 1:5 in acid
chapters.script: Dichromate contains two chromium atoms, each at plus six. Reducing both to plus three requires three electrons per chromium, giving six per dichromate ion. Iron two plus supplies one electron when it becomes iron three plus. Therefore zero point zero one zero zero mole of dichromate can oxidize zero point zero six zero zero mole of iron two plus under the stated acidic reaction. Permanganate becoming manganese two plus instead accepts five electrons per ion. Zero point zero two zero zero mole can therefore oxidize zero point one zero zero mole of iron two plus. Check charge as well as the mole ratio. In the acidic permanganate half equation, minus one plus eight minus five equals plus two, matching the product charge. For dichromate, minus two plus fourteen minus six equals plus six, matching two chromium three plus ions. Water and hydrogen ions must also balance oxygen and hydrogen atoms. These checks distinguish a correct acidic equation from a memorized electron factor used with the wrong product or medium.
points: 0.0100 mol Cr₂O₇²⁻ · × 6 · 0.0600 mol

chapters.title: Track oxidation from chromite to chromate
chapters.script: Preparation equations become easier to understand when oxidation numbers are checked alongside atom balance. Chromite has formula iron chromium two oxygen four, with iron two and chromium three in the elementary oxidation state description. In the stated oxidative carbonate conversion, chromium becomes plus six in chromate while iron becomes plus three in iron oxide. The balanced equation uses four chromite units, eight sodium carbonate units and seven oxygen molecules, giving eight sodium chromate, two iron oxide and eight carbon dioxide units. Eight chromium atoms each lose three electrons, while four iron atoms each lose one, making twenty eight electrons transferred. Seven oxygen molecules accept that total when oxygen changes from zero to minus two. Carbon remains plus four, so carbonate is not the redox donor merely because carbon dioxide appears. The sodium chromate product supplies the chromium containing intermediate for subsequent dichromate chemistry. Check chromium, iron, sodium, carbon and oxygen independently before deciding coefficients. These equations summarize chemical principles and the relationship between ore and product, rather than specifying an operational preparation method or claiming that the solid mixture behaves as a simple aqueous ionic reaction.
points: Cr: +3 → +6 · 8 atoms × 3 electrons · 24 electrons lost
Fe: +2 → +3 · 4 atoms × 1 electron · 4 electrons lost
O₂: 7 molecules · 7 × 4 electrons accepted · 28 electrons balanced

chapters.title: Chromate and dichromate interconvert without redox
chapters.script: Chromate and dichromate provide a useful distinction between acid base equilibrium and oxidation reduction. Their interconversion can be written as two chromate ions plus two hydrogen ions giving one dichromate ion and water, with a reversible arrow. Chromium remains in oxidation state plus six on both sides. Acidification therefore changes the balance between these species without requiring electrons in the net equation. In the common qualitative comparison, chromate is yellow and dichromate orange. Increasing hydroxide concentration consumes hydrogen ions and favours chromate within the stated equilibrium conditions. A basic form of the reverse conversion uses one dichromate plus two hydroxides to give two chromates and one water. Charge is minus four on each side of that equation. The preparation of potassium dichromate can exploit the lower solubility of its salt relative to the corresponding sodium salt under the specified crystallization conditions; it is not explained by changing chromium's oxidation number during salt exchange. Actual speciation depends on concentration and acidity, so the two ion equation is an organizing model rather than a claim that every chromium six solution contains only one species of a single colour.
points: Acid-favoured comparison · 2CrO₄²⁻ + 2H⁺ ⇌ Cr₂O₇²⁻ + H₂O · Yellow ↔ orange
Basic reverse · Cr₂O₇²⁻ + 2OH⁻ → 2CrO₄²⁻ + H₂O · Charges: −4 each side
Chromium oxidation state · +6 in both ions · No electron transfer

chapters.title: Distinguish manganate from permanganate preparation
chapters.script: Manganate and permanganate differ by one unit of ionic charge and one unit of manganese oxidation state. The green manganate ion has manganese plus six, while the purple permanganate ion has manganese plus seven. In the usual preparation scheme, manganese dioxide is first converted under alkaline oxidizing conditions to manganate. An electrolytic oxidation can then remove one electron per manganate to form permanganate. The oxidation half equation is manganate giving permanganate plus an electron; oxygen atom count is unchanged. Manganate can also undergo disproportionation under suitable less strongly basic conditions. The balanced acidic representation uses three manganate ions and four hydrogen ions to form two permanganate ions, one manganese dioxide and two waters. Two manganese centres rise from six to seven, losing two electrons in total, while one falls from six to four and gains two. This is not simply a colour change caused by dilution. State the chemical conditions and distinguish oxidation of all manganate from simultaneous oxidation and reduction of different manganese centres. These are reaction relationships for interpreting preparation chemistry, not a laboratory recipe or a claim that every solution follows the same pathway regardless of p H.
points: Manganate → permanganate · Mn(+6) → Mn(+7) · Lose 1 electron per Mn
Disproportionation: 3 Mn(+6) · 2 rise to +7; 1 falls to +4 · 2 electrons lost and gained
Net acidic representation · 3MnO₄²⁻ + 4H⁺ → 2MnO₄⁻ + MnO₂ + 2H₂O · Atoms and charge balanced

chapters.title: The permanganate product fixes the electron factor
chapters.script: The electron factor of permanganate is not one fixed number independent of the product. In the familiar sufficiently acidic reduction to manganese two, manganese changes from plus seven to plus two and accepts five electrons. A balanced acidic half equation also consumes eight hydrogen ions and forms four waters. When the specified reduction product is manganese dioxide, manganese ends at plus four and accepts three electrons. A basic half equation uses permanganate, two waters and three electrons to form manganese dioxide and four hydroxides. When the stated strongly alkaline comparison gives manganate, manganese ends at plus six and accepts one electron, with the same four oxygen atoms. For one millimole permanganate, those three product assumptions correspond to five, three or one millimole electrons. Consequently an equivalent mass or a titration ratio must refer to the actual product and reaction conditions. Medium influences products, but the reducing agent, concentration and kinetics also matter; a p H label alone does not guarantee the same outcome for every reaction. Balance atoms and total charge after selecting the stated product instead of memorizing an electron factor without its chemical context.
points: MnO₄⁻ → Mn²⁺ · +7 to +2 · 5 electrons per Mn
MnO₄⁻ → MnO₂ · +7 to +4 · 3 electrons per Mn
MnO₄⁻ → MnO₄²⁻ · +7 to +6 · 1 electron per Mn

chapters.title: Count selected lanthanoid f configurations
chapters.script: Selected lanthanoid oxidation states become clearer when the actual ion configuration is written. Cerium three has one electron in the four f subshell in the usual ionic description, while cerium four has an empty four f subshell. Europium three has six four f electrons, and europium two has seven, giving a half filled four f set. Ytterbium three has thirteen four f electrons, while ytterbium two has fourteen and a filled set. A four f subshell contains seven spatial orbitals and at most fourteen electrons. In the elementary Hund filling picture, the half filled seven electron set has one electron in each orbital, whereas the fourteen electron set has all seven pairs. Empty, half filled or filled arrangements can help rationalize particular oxidation state patterns, but electronic bookkeeping alone does not determine stability in every chemical environment. Lattice, hydration and redox energies also contribute. Do not assume that the common plus three state gives the same f count for every element or that every lanthanoid readily exhibits all these alternatives. The purpose of the comparison is to connect element identity, ionic charge and occupancy before discussing periodic trends or magnetic evidence.
points: Cerium comparison · Ce³⁺: 4f¹ → Ce⁴⁺: 4f⁰ · Empty 4f in Ce⁴⁺
Europium comparison · Eu³⁺: 4f⁶ → Eu²⁺: 4f⁷ · Half-filled 4f in Eu²⁺
Ytterbium comparison · Yb³⁺: 4f¹³ → Yb²⁺: 4f¹⁴ · Filled 4f in Yb²⁺

chapters.title: Actinoid charge and f counts need a stated model
chapters.script: Actinoid configurations require specifying the actual species rather than copying a neutral atom label onto every ion. Use the supplied elementary neutral uranium configuration with a radon core, three five f electrons, one six d electron and two seven s electrons. In the simple isolated ion bookkeeping used here, forming uranium four plus removes four outer electrons: the two seven s electrons, the six d electron and one five f electron. The remaining count is five f two. The corresponding formal six plus uranium count is five f zero in this model. Now consider the uranyl ion, containing uranium and two oxygens, with overall charge plus two. Assigning each oxygen minus two makes uranium oxidation state plus six, despite the whole ion having charge plus two. Formal oxidation states and actual molecular electron density are different descriptions, so this does not claim that uranyl consists of a free bare uranium six plus ion. More detailed actinoid bonding includes covalency and closely spaced orbitals. Read overall charge, ligand oxidation assignments and the specified electron-count model separately before reporting an f configuration.

chapters.title: Two d4 ions can have different redox roles
chapters.script: Matching d electron counts do not guarantee matching redox behaviour. Chromium two plus and manganese three plus both have a formal d four count, yet their supplied aqueous reduction potentials differ. Use minus zero point four one volt for chromium three plus accepting one electron to become chromium two plus, and plus one point five one volts for manganese three plus accepting one electron to become manganese two plus. Combining manganese reduction with chromium two plus oxidation gives manganese three plus plus chromium two plus forming manganese two plus plus chromium three plus. The standard cell potential is one point five one minus minus zero point four one, or plus one point nine two volts. One electron is transferred per written reaction. With supplied Faraday constant ninety six thousand four hundred eighty five coulombs per mole, standard Gibbs energy change is approximately minus one hundred eighty five kilojoules per mole of reaction. The resulting d five manganese two plus and d three chromium three plus counts help organize the comparison, but measured potentials include the full specified chemical environment. Complexation, concentration and p H can change an actual redox comparison.
points: Cr³⁺ + e⁻ → Cr²⁺ · Supplied E°red = −0.41 V · Reverse this step for oxidation
Mn³⁺ + e⁻ → Mn²⁺ · Supplied E°red = +1.51 V · Manganese reduction

chapters.title: Carbide composition is not an alloy property prediction
chapters.formula: Fe₃C with supplied Fe=56, C=12: carbon mass fraction = 12/180
chapters.script: A carbide formula can support a composition calculation without determining every property of an alloy. Cementite has the formula iron three carbide, with three iron atoms for each carbon atom. Using supplied atomic masses iron fifty six and carbon twelve gives formula mass one hundred eighty grams per mole. The carbon mass fraction is twelve divided by one hundred eighty, or about six point six seven percent. Thus one point eight zero grams of pure ideal cementite contains zero point one two zero gram carbon and one point six eight grams iron. Now use a stipulated two component mass model containing ten percent cementite and ninety percent pure iron. Since the pure iron component contributes no carbon, overall carbon percentage is one tenth of the cementite carbon percentage, about zero point six six seven percent. This does not mean a real steel is always described by only those two components or that hardness is a linear function of carbon fraction. Microstructure, phase distribution and processing also matter. Count formula units and mass fractions before connecting a composition to any independently supplied materials-property data.
points: Fe₃C formula mass · 3×56 + 12 · 180 g/mol
Pure cementite carbon fraction · 12/180 · 6.67% by mass
Ideal mixture: 10% Fe₃C, rest Fe · 0.10×6.67% · About 0.667% total carbon

chapters.title: Chromium oxide acidity changes with oxidation state
chapters.formula: CrO: Cr(II); Cr₂O₃: Cr(III); CrO₃: Cr(VI)
chapters.script: Oxide acid base behaviour can vary across oxidation states of the same transition element. In the introductory chromium comparison, chromium two oxide is mainly basic, chromium three oxide is amphoteric, and chromium six oxide is acidic. Charge balance gives chromium oxidation states plus two in the monoxide, plus three in the two chromium three oxygen formula, and plus six in the trioxide. A simple acid reaction for the monoxide uses two hydrogen ions to give chromium two ions and water. For chromium three oxide, six hydrogen ions give two chromium three ions and three waters. Amphoteric behaviour also requires reaction with suitable base conditions; its products depend on the stated medium. Chromium trioxide can react with two hydroxide ions to give a chromate ion and water, with chromium remaining plus six. This last equation is acid base conversion, not a chromium oxidation state change. The comparison illustrates a useful trend toward acidic oxides at higher oxidation state, rather than a universal classification rule for every transition metal compound. Keep oxide formula, oxidation state, reaction medium and redox classification as separate checks.
points: CrO; Cr₂O₃; CrO₃ · Cr oxidation states +2, +3, +6 · Basic; amphoteric; acidic
Cr₂O₃ + 6H⁺ · → 2Cr³⁺ + 3H₂O · Atom and charge balance
CrO₃ + 2OH⁻ · → CrO₄²⁻ + H₂O · Cr stays +6; acid–base conversion
